title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
claim: A controlled benchmark isolates basic visual skills, each varied independently with explicit rule-based values, to test generalization in a systematic way.
layout: 6 panels in one row, one skill per panel, labeled titles
description: A single horizontal row of six equal square panels with rounded black borders. A title sits above each panel: Size, Position, Rotation, Count, Shape and Color. Every panel uses a simple flat shape on a white background, drawn in saturated orange against a pale peach ghost of the same object. The ghost marks a different skill value. Size shows a large orange circle inside a larger peach circle. Position shows an orange circle overlapping a peach circle that sits slightly to its right. Rotation shows an orange arrow over a faint peach arrow at a slightly different angle. Count shows two orange circles and one peach circle. Shape shows an orange circle inside a peach triangle. Color shows a circle split diagonally into blue and peach halves. The eye goes first to the bright orange shapes, then along the row of skill titles.
caption: The Visual Generative Lab (VGL). VGL trains diffusion models from scratch on synthetic renders labeled with explicit skill values. Each panel varies one skill while holding the others fixed. Models are trained on a subset of skill values or combinations and evaluated on unseen ones within or beyond the training range.
abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as FrÃ©chet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.
